newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's parliament adds voice to anti-ETA outcry.
newsitem.headline: Spain's parliament adds voice to anti-ETA outcry.

text.p: Spain's parliament on Thursday unanimously condemned Basque separatist group ETA for its killing of a young town councillor and promised to take action against guerrilla violence.

Adding its voice to the public outcry against ETA's assassination of 29-year-old Miguel Angel Blanco, parliament issued a declaration praising Spaniards for taking to the streets and "overcoming fear of those who wield guns and those who support them".

Ruling Popular Party deputy Fernando Trillo, Speaker of Congress, said parliament "understands that terrorist acts cannot have any other response than to deepen the unity of society and its democratic institutions."
Spanish lawmakers also gave their backing to the government's efforts to clamp down on ETA, which kidnapped Blanco on Thursday and shot him 48 hours later.

The Basque government, with enthusiastic support from Madrid, on Wednesday barred ETA's political wing Herri Batasuna from going ahead with a planned demonstration on Saturday in San Sebastian for fear it would ignite more violence in the region.
A Herri Batasuna spokesman said he did not know if the group would go ahead with the demonstration despite the ban.
Basque officials also prohibited a second pro-ETA rally that was expected to take place within days of the first.
Basque politicial leaders and the central government in Madrid have vowed to isolate Herri Batasuna because it did not condemn the killing, which sparked national outrage.
Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar's government has promised a crackdown on the separatist rebels and is formulating tougher legislation to combat terrorism.
"There are legal steps we must take (against ETA)," Interior Minister Jaime Mayor Oreja told reporters on Wednesday. "We will be steadfast in applying those measures."
The proposed reforms, which must be approved by parliament, include criminalising demonstrations by activists who mask their faces, and banning counter-demonstrations against pacifist groups.
The government also wants to increase the jail terms for threats or any action construed as "defence of terrorism".

Spaniards, shocked by the killing of such an ordinary low-level functionary, have mounted huge street protests against ETA. The government estimates that six million people have demonstrated across the country since Blanco's death on Sunday.

Though almost all the gatherings were peaceful, scattered clashes have erupted between ETA supporters and opponents around the Basque country. There have also been a number of attempts to burn Herri Batasuna offices.
Basques were once intimidated by the radical separatists but have become newly emboldened by the nationwide condemnation.
Aznar told parliament he saw the street demonstrations as a call for government action.
"It's the responsibility of all democrats, political parties and all public institutions and social forces to carry out the response that society demands," he said.
However, too tough a crackdown could play into the hands of ETA by generating public sympathy for its claims that the government is authoritarian and violates human rights, analysts say.
And ETA has already shown its defiance of the public opinion by threatening a second Basque town councillor with death.
ETA began its armed campaign for an independent state in 1968 under the dictatorship of Francisco Franco, who repressed any expression of Basque nationalism.

Support for the group has waned since Franco's death in 1975 and the subsequent transition to democracy, which eventually gave the Basque region a high degree of autonomy. The rebels have killed about 800 people in their 29-year struggle.

As condemnation of ETA mounts, there are signs of a rift in the radical camp. A growing number of ETA prisoners and Herri Batasuna members are speaking out against Blanco's killing and questioning the wisdom of continued armed struggle.
